title: Fill in the Blanks
summary: One sentence, one or two blanks, four options — decided almost always by a collocation, a phrasal unit, a tense anchor or a confusable pair, not by dictionary size. Every blank has a governor (a word beside it) that dictates the answer; finding that governor first is the whole technique.

subtopics.title: Collocation blanks: word partnerships that decide the answer
subtopics.concept:
A collocation is a pair of words that native usage glues together. When a blank sits beside a verb or an adjective, the answer is usually whatever that word *partners* with — not any word of similar meaning.

| Verb + noun | Adjective + noun | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pay attention / compliments | staunch supporter | loyal follower |
| strike a balance / a bargain | soaring prices | rising fast |
| break the news / a record | grave mistake / crisis | very serious |
| take place / pride / measures | scathing attack | bitterly critical |
| make efforts / amends | teeming millions | crowds of people |
| do business / justice / harm | invaluable service | too valuable to price |
| commit a mistake / a crime | abject poverty | utter, hopeless |
| reach a conclusion / a consensus | conclusive evidence | settling the issue |
| cast a vote / a glance | close scrutiny | careful examination |
| lay emphasis / claim / hands on | level playing field | fair conditions |
| gain ground / momentum | glaring error | shockingly obvious |
| bear fruit / a resemblance | barren land / effort | unproductive |

**How to use the governor.** Identify the word immediately governing the blank:
- blank after a verb → the verb's usual object (*break the news*, *take place*);
- blank before a noun → the noun's usual adjective (*grave mistake*, *close scrutiny*);
- blank after a noun → its usual verb (*prices soar*, *attention pays*? — attention takes *pay*).

**Why collocation beats meaning.** 'made a mistake' and 'committed a mistake' both 'make sense', but SSC's standard answer follows the strongest partnership (*commit a mistake*, *commit a crime*). Similarly *reach* a conclusion (not *arrive* a conclusion), *pay* attention (not *give* attention), *heavy* rain (not *strong* rain).

**Register check.** When two partnerships both exist, the neutral-formal one fits SSC prose: *hold talks* beats *hold chats*; *offer condolences* beats *give sorrows* (which is not even an English partnership).

Build your pairing instinct in two weeks: one table of 10 pairs a day, and each pair immediately used in a sentence of your own. Recognition in the exam comes from *having produced* the pair once, not from having read it.

tricks.title: Governor-first reading
tricks.body: Read the sentence up to the blank, stop, and ask: 'What does this word usually take next?' Answer from memory, then look at the options — your answer is usually sitting there verbatim.

example.q: The two leaders held detailed ___ on the border dispute.
example.solution: 'held detailed...' asks for a discussion noun → *deliberations*. Celebrations/medications are topic-inappropriate; 'reverberations' is sound.

tricks.title: Topic veto
tricks.body: Collocation options in SSC are often same-suffix decoys (-tions, -ments). Kill them by topic first: a border dispute invites *talks/deliberations*, never *medications*.

tricks.title: Verb-object completeness
tricks.body: For verb blanks, complete the object in your head: 'attention is ___' → paid. If your completing verb is an option, mark it and move on.

mistakes: Choosing a synonym that breaks the partnership ('pay attention' → 'give attention').
Being impressed by long words; the collocation answer is usually the ordinary word.
Ignoring the preposition that follows the blank ('deliberations on', 'effect on').
Confusing adjective–noun order: the blank's side tells you its part of speech.

subtopics.title: Phrasal-verb blanks: verb + particle as one unit
subtopics.concept:
A phrasal verb is verb + particle(s) whose meaning is not the sum of its parts. Blanks here test whether you own the unit.

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Sentence cue |
|---|---|---|
| call off | cancel | the strike was called off |
| put up with | tolerate | she cannot put up with noise |
| carry out | perform, execute | carry out orders / a survey |
| break out | begin suddenly | a fire broke out |
| look into | investigate | the panel will look into it |
| turn down | reject | he turned down the offer |
| give in | surrender | the rebels finally gave in |
| run out of | exhaust the stock of | we ran out of time |
| do away with | abolish | the tax was done away with |
| bring about | cause to happen | the reform brought about change |
| cut down on | reduce | cut down on sugar |
| stand by | support; remain loyal | she stood by her friend |

**Two shapes of the blank.** Sometimes the particle is blanked ('call ___ the merger') and the verb is given; sometimes the whole unit is blanked among look-alike verbs ('___ up with the noise'). In both, the sentence's *action* decides:
- cancelling → call **off**;
- enduring → put **up with**;
- rejecting → turn **down**;
- abolishing → do away **with**.

**Particles carry direction.** *off* = cancel/away, *out* = erupt/distribute, *up* = appear/build, *down* = reject/reduce, *in* = surrender/enter. When two particles both look grammatical, this direction sense separates them.

**Transitive or not.** *Put up with* needs an object ('put up with the noise'); *give in* needs none ('the rebels gave in'). If the blank follows a ready object, a transitive unit is the answer; if the sentence ends at the blank, an intransitive one.

**Separable units.** 'called the meeting off' and 'called off the meeting' are both valid — so if the object sits between the blank's verb and particle, the unit is separable, and only that shape fits. Improvement items exploit this; fill-in items usually keep the unit intact.

tricks.title: Name the action, then match the unit
tricks.body: Say the sentence's action in one plain word (cancelled, tolerated, abolished), then pick the phrasal unit that translates it. The wrong particles translate other actions.

example.q: The company had to call ___ the proposed merger after the audit.
example.solution: Action = cancel → call **off**. *Call up* telephones, *call for* demands, *call out* shouts — different verbs entirely.

tricks.title: Particle direction check
tricks.body: Ask what the sentence does to its object — kills it (off/out), raises it (up), lowers it (down), accepts it (in). Match the particle's direction to the verb's fate.

tricks.title: Simple-verb substitution
tricks.body: Replace each option with a one-word verb (call off = cancel). The option whose substitution keeps the sentence's meaning is the answer.

mistakes: Choosing the particle that follows the preposition logic of the first language.
Mixing *put up with* (tolerate) with *put off* (postpone) because both contain 'put'.
Reading only the clause containing the blank; the actor and time usually sit in the previous clause.
Forgetting that 'break out' (war, fire, disease) has no passive — 'was broken out' is impossible.

subtopics.title: Verb-form and tense blanks
subtopics.concept:
When the blank is a verb, two checks decide: the **anchor** (time information in the sentence) and the **form demanded by the governing word**.

**Anchors → tenses:**
- *By the time X arrived, ...* → the earlier event is past perfect: *had burnt*.
- *since 2015 / for ten years* (continuing) → present perfect (continuous).
- *yesterday / last week* → simple past.
- *by next March* → future perfect: *will have completed*.

**Governing words → forms (the highest-yield list):**
- *look forward to + -ing* (to = preposition): *I look forward to **hearing** from you*.
- *used to + base* (past habit) vs *be used to + -ing* (accustomed): *He used to **swim***; *He is used to **swimming***.
- *had better / would rather + base*: *You had better **leave***.
- *avoid / enjoy / mind / finish / suggest + -ing*.
- *decide / plan / hope / refuse + to + base*.
- preposition + -ing: *insisted on **paying***, *afraid of **losing***.

**The preposition-to test** settles most -ing vs to-blank confusion: if the word before 'to' is a noun, pronoun or preposition-like verb (look forward, be accustomed, object), the 'to' is prepositional → *-ing* follows. If 'to' belongs to an infinitive (decide, refuse, hope), the base verb follows.

**Passive shapes** also appear: after *by the time*, a completed earlier event can be *had been + participle* when the subject receives the action (*had been evacuated*).

tricks.title: Preposition-to test
tricks.body: Check what owns the 'to'. Owned by a preposition-verb or noun → -ing; owned by an infinitive verb → base form. This one test answers the largest tense-form family.

example.q: I look forward to ___ from you soon. → hearing
example.solution: 'Forward to' is prepositional ('look forward to it'), so the -ing form follows: *hearing*.

tricks.title: By-the-time ladder
tricks.body: Two events with 'by the time' → earlier verb in past perfect, later in simple past. Fit the blank to its rung of the ladder.

tricks.title: Verb-category lists
tricks.body: Memorise the three mini-lists: -ing verbs (avoid, enjoy, mind, suggest, finish), to-verbs (decide, hope, refuse, plan), base-after (had better, would rather, let, make).

mistakes: Choosing 'to hear' after 'look forward to' because 'to' feels infinitive.
Using present perfect with a finished-time anchor.
Writing 'used to + -ing' for past habits (that shape means 'accustomed').
Ignoring the passive when the sentence's subject receives the action.

subtopics.title: Connective and relative-pronoun blanks
subtopics.concept:
Connective blanks join two clauses; the relation between the clauses, not the meaning of any single word, is the answer.

| Pair | Fixed shape | Trap option |
|---|---|---|
| Hardly / Scarcely ... when | Hardly had she entered **when** the lights went out. | **than** (belongs to no sooner) |
| No sooner ... than | No sooner had he sat down **than**... | **when** |
| Not only ... but also | not only cheap **but also** durable | but, and |
| Both ... and | **Both** the manager **and** his staff were present | as well as |
| Rather ... than | would resign **rather than** apologize | then |
| Too ... to | **too** weak **to** walk | so, very |
| So ... that | **so** weak **that** he could not walk | too |
| Lest ... should | run fast **lest** you **should** miss it | or else |

**The +/- test again:** give each clause a direction. Same directions → *so/therefore/and*; opposite → *but/yet/although*; explanation → *because/since*; outcome → *so/therefore*. For fixed pairs, both halves must appear: 'Hardly had... **when**', 'No sooner had... **than**' — the trap options simply swap the partners.

**Relative pronouns.** The blank joining a describing clause to its noun:
- person + subject role → **who** (*the leader **who** inspires*);
- person + object role → **whom** (*the leader **whom** everyone trusts* — test by rephrasing: *everyone trusts him*);
- possession → **whose**; things → **which/that**;
- place → **where**; time → **when**; reason → **why**.
The he/him substitution is foolproof: replace the pronoun's slot with he (→ who) or him (→ whom).

**Concessive pairs:** *Although/Though* pairs with *yet* (never *but*): 'Although it rained, **yet** the match continued' is standard formal usage; SSC accepts plain 'Although... the match continued' equally. *Despite/In spite of* take noun/-ing, never a full clause ('despite it rained' is wrong).

tricks.title: Partner scan before choosing
tricks.body: Search the sentence for the other half of the pair. Seeing 'Hardly had' fixes the blank to *when*; seeing 'No sooner' fixes it to *than*. Zero deliberation needed.

example.q: Hardly had she entered the room ___ the lights went out.

tricks.title: He/him substitution for who/whom
tricks.body: Rephrase the clause with he/him: 'everyone trusts (him)' → whom; '(he) inspires everyone' → who. No ambiguity survives the substitution.

tricks.title: Despite/Although sorting
tricks.body: Full clause after the blank → Although/Though; noun or -ing → Despite/In spite of. The trap options swap these two families.

mistakes: Choosing 'than' after 'Hardly/Scarcely' because 'comparison' instinct fires.
Using 'whom' as a clause subject ('the man whom came') — case is decided by the clause role, not by prestige.
Joining a full clause with 'despite' or a bare noun with 'although'.
Selecting 'which' for a person or 'who' for a thing under time pressure.

subtopics.title: Confusable and homonym blanks
subtopics.concept:
These blanks offer four words of similar shape; only one fits both the grammar slot and the meaning.

| Pair | Meanings | Correct use |
|---|---|---|
| affect / effect | verb: influence / noun: result | Rains **affect** crops; the **effect** was visible. |
| advice / advise | noun (an advice) / verb (to advise) | The doctor **advised** rest; follow his **advice**. |
| practice / practise | noun (Indian English) / verb | Daily **practice** helps; **practise** daily. |
| principal / principle | chief, head / a rule | **Principal** amount; a man of **principle**. |
| stationary / stationery | not moving / writing materials | a **stationary** van; office **stationery**. |
| loose / lose | not tight / misplace | a **loose** tooth; **lose** the keys. |
| site / sight / cite | place / vision / quote | a construction **site**; at first **sight**; **cite** a case. |
| complement / compliment | completes / praise | wine **complements** food; pay a **compliment**. |
| discreet / discrete | careful / separate | **discreet** enquiries; **discrete** units. |
| eligible / illegible | qualified / unreadable | **eligible** voters; **illegible** signature. |
| beside / besides | next to / in addition to | sat **beside** me; **besides** swimming. |
| assure / ensure / insure | remove doubt / make certain / cover by policy | **assure** the public; **ensure** safety; **insure** the car. |
| lie / lay | recline (lie–lay–lain) / put (lay–laid) | **lie** down; **lay** the pen on the table. |

**Two-step decision.**
1. **Part of speech.** *advise* (verb) vs *advice* (noun): find the sentence's verb — if it already has one, the blank is likely a noun, and vice versa. Same for *practice/practise*, *effect/affect* (noun vs verb).
2. **Meaning.** *stationary* (not moving) vs *stationery* (writing material); *principal* (chief) vs *principle* (rule). The sentence's context — a godown of paper goods, a bank's sums — picks one.

**Spelling-distinct pairs with one meaning slot:** *eligible* (qualified) vs *illegible* (unreadable); *discreet* (careful) vs *discrete* (separate); *complement* (completes) vs *compliment* (praise). Meaning decides alone.

**The assure/ensure/insure family** deserves its own memorisation: *assure* a person (remove doubt), *ensure* an outcome (make certain), *insure* a thing (insurance policy). 'The minister gave a solemn **assurance**' is the noun of *assure* — options include *insurance* to trap the shape-reader.

**Sound-alike traps in options** (affection, effectiveness, advices) exist to punish incomplete reading: reject them on grammar ('advices' is not a countable noun in standard English) and on meaning.

tricks.title: Slot first, meaning second
tricks.body: Decide noun/verb/adjective from the sentence frame; kill every option of the wrong class. Then choose by meaning among survivors — usually only two ever reach step two.

example.q: The doctor ___ him to take complete rest. Options: advised / advice / advices / advise.
example.solution: The sentence needs a finite past verb (subject 'doctor', no other verb) → **advised**. *Advice* is a noun, *advices* is not standard, *advise* is the wrong tense/number fit here.

tricks.title: Context picture
tricks.body: Form a mental image of the sentence: a pile of paper in a godown → stationery; a parked van → stationary. The image picks the spelling instantly.

tricks.title: Triple-family cards
tricks.body: Make flash cards only for families of three or more: assure/ensure/insure, site/sight/cite, affect/effect/affective. Singles rarely appear in options.

mistakes: Choosing the familiar spelling ('affect') when the slot demands the noun ('effect').
Reading 'advice/advise' as interchangeable because dictionaries mark the Indian-English overlap.
Picking 'illegible' for eligibility contexts because the negative prefix sounds right.
Missing that the sentence already has a verb, so the blank must be a noun.

subtopics.title: Double blanks: two gaps, one sentence
subtopics.concept:
Some items blank two positions in one sentence — a pair of connectors (*___ he was ill, ___ he came*), a structure pair (*too ... to*, *so ... that*), or two content words. Options are complete pairs.

**Method: anchor the solid blank first.** One of the two gaps is usually much easier — a structure pair whose second element is fixed (*too ___ to*), or a content word only one option can fit. Decide that gap, and the wrong pairs collapse:
- '*___ small ___ accommodate*' → the structure is *too + adj + to + verb* → **too, to**. 'So, that' would need a clause ('so small that it could not accommodate'), and the option's second element ('that') does not fit the blank before the bare verb.
- '*___ the manager ___ his assistants were present*' → plural *were* + two-part subject → **Both, and**. 'Neither, or' is not a pair; 'Either, or' would demand singular agreement.

**Agreement as a tiebreak.** The sentence's verb exposes the pair: plural verb → *both... and* (or a plural pair), singular verb → *either... or / neither... nor* (verb follows the nearer noun).

**Cross-check both halves.** After anchoring one blank, read the completed sentence aloud; if the second half jars, your anchor was the trap — the option pairs are built so that exactly one completes both halves naturally.

**Content-word pairs** (e.g. '*safe and sound*', '*part and parcel*') are fixed binomials — learn the common ones in pairs, never singly: *safe and sound, first and foremost, null and void, ways and means, pros and cons, part and parcel*.

tricks.title: Structure-pair recognition
tricks.body: too + adjective + to + base verb; so + adjective + that + clause; such + noun + that + clause; hardly...when; no sooner...than. Recognise the skeleton and both blanks fill at once.

example.q: The room was ___ small ___ accommodate all the guests.
example.solution: Adjective + bare verb after the second blank → *too small to accommodate*. 'So, that' would demand 'that it could not accommodate'.

tricks.title: Verb-agreement tiebreak
tricks.body: Plural verb with two subjects → Both...and; singular verb → Either...or / Neither...nor (matching the nearer noun). The verb alone often fixes the pair.

tricks.title: Fixed binomial bank
tricks.body: Revise binomials in pairs: safe and sound, part and parcel, null and void, first and foremost, ways and means. Options split genuine binomials with a wrong partner — the genuine one is the answer.

mistakes: Solving blank two first when blank one is the structural anchor.
Choosing 'so, that' where the second blank precedes a bare verb (structure mismatch).
Matching plural 'Both...and' to a singular-verb sentence.
Assembling a binomial that half-exists ('part and half') because the first half matched.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Blank sits beside a verb or adjective; options are same-suffix nouns/verbs of related meaning.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the governor, recall its usual partner, veto decoys by topic and suffix.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options differ by spelling or suffix: advice/advise, effect/affect, stationery/stationary, eligible/illegible.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the part of speech from the frame first, then pick by meaning; reject non-standard forms outright.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options are particles (off/out/up) or short verb units (look into, carry out) around a clear action.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name the action in plain words, then match the unit; check particle direction and transitivity.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Blank is a verb; anchors like 'by the time', 'since', 'yesterday' or governing words like 'look forward to' are visible.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor fixes the tense; the preposition-to test fixes -ing vs base form.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two blanks per sentence, options are pairs such as 'Both, and' / 'too, to' / 'Although, called off'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor the easier gap (usually the structural half), let it eliminate pairs, then cross-check the second half.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Blank joins two clauses (Hardly... ___, Although... ___) or a relative clause (the leader ___ everyone trusts).
pyqPatterns.approach: Use clause relation and fixed partners for connectives; he/him substitution for who/whom.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The manager managed to ___ a balance between the two demanding clients.
solvedExamples.solution: The fixed partnership is **strike a balance** (= find a middle position). *Knock/break/pull a balance* are not English partnerships — the options are ordinary verbs placed to test pairing memory, not meaning.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Recall the partnership, not the dictionary: balance → strike.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The villagers could no longer put ___ with the erratic power supply.
solvedExamples.solution: The sentence needs 'tolerate': **put up with**. *Put on* wears, *put off* postpones, *put in* installs — each particle builds a different verb. The cue 'could no longer' + a nuisance noun demands the tolerate-unit.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Name the action (tolerate) and match the unit: tolerate = put up with.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ the students ___ the teacher was aware of the change in schedule.
solvedExamples.solution: The verb *was* is singular. 'Both...and' demands a plural verb (*were*), and 'Neither, or' is not a pair. With *Either...or*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject — *the teacher* (singular) → **was**, exactly as the sentence reads. 'Not only, but' is incomplete without 'also'.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Verb agreement decides the pair: singular was after a two-part subject → Either...or (nearer subject singular).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The two leaders held detailed ___ on the border dispute.
practice.solution: 'Held detailed ___ on a dispute' asks for the discussion partnership: **deliberations**. The other options share the -tion shape but belong to wrong topics — parties celebrate, patients take medication, sound reverberates.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The new taxation policy will have a far-reaching ___ on small traders.
practice.solution: After the article *a* the blank must be a noun, and the meaning is 'result': **effect**. *Affect* is the verb; *affection* is fondness; *effectiveness* needs no 'a far-reaching' frame and changes the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The company had to call ___ the proposed merger after the audit report.
practice.solution: Action = cancel: **call off**. *Call up* telephones, *call out* challenges/announces, *call for* demands — none survives the substitution test.
practice.shortcut: Substitute 'cancel' — the surviving particle is off.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The retired professor could not put ___ with the constant construction noise.
practice.solution: Tolerate = **put up with**, a three-word unit whose object follows ('with the noise'). *Put on/off/in/across* build other meanings — wear, postpone, install, communicate.
practice.shortcut: Nuisance + 'could not' → tolerate → put up with.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

By the time the firefighters arrived, the wooden shed ___ to ashes.
practice.solution: 'By the time + past event' makes the blank the earlier of two past actions → past perfect: **had burnt**. Present-perfect options clash with the past anchor, and 'was burning' describes a mid-process rather than the completed ruin.
practice.shortcut: By-the-time ladder: earlier event → had + participle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I look forward to ___ from you at the earliest.
practice.solution: 'Look forward to' is prepositional ('forward to it'), so the -ing form follows: **hearing**. The other options serve an infinitive or passive slot that this frame does not have.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ it rained heavily throughout the day, the final match was not ___.
practice.solution: The clauses contrast (rain vs the match happening) → concession: **Although** — this eliminates both 'Because' pairs. A match that is not played is **called off**; *called on* visits, *called up* telephones. Only the first pair completes both halves.
practice.shortcut: Anchor the connective (contrast → Although), then match the phrasal to the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Hardly had the chief guest taken his seat ___ the curtains rose.
practice.solution: 'Hardly had...' partners with **when**: 'Hardly had X happened when Y happened'. *Than* belongs exclusively to 'No sooner...than'.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The paediatrician ___ the mother to complete the full course of medicine.
practice.solution: The sentence needs a finite past verb after its subject: **advised**. *Advice* is a noun, *advices* is not standard English, *advising* cannot serve alone as the verb.
practice.shortcut: Frame first: subject + blank + object → finite verb → advised.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

All the ___ items — pens, registers and markers — were locked in the storeroom.
practice.solution: Pens, registers and markers are writing materials: **stationery**. *Stationary* means not moving — the items may be stationary too, but the apposition with the list pins the meaning to the writing-materials word.
practice.shortcut: Context picture: pens and registers → stationery.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The union leader ___ every worker trusts was re-elected without a contest.
practice.solution: Rephrase the clause: 'every worker trusts (him)' — object role, person → **whom**. *Whose* shows possession, *which* serves things, *what* does not introduce such relative clauses.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The Principal congratulated the debate team ___ winning the national championship.
practice.solution: The fixed partnership is **congratulate on**: 'congratulated the team on winning'. The -ing after the blank is exactly what this frame expects.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The auditorium was ___ small ___ accommodate the entire graduating batch.
practice.solution: Adjective + bare verb after the second blank → the *too + adj + to + base verb* structure: **too small to accommodate**. 'So, that' would need a full clause ('so small that it could not accommodate'), 'very' forms no pair, and 'too, for' needs a noun after 'for'.
practice.shortcut: Recognise the skeleton: too + adj + to + verb.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ the manager ___ his assistants were responsible for the filing error.
practice.solution: The verb *were* is plural, and 'Both...and' is the only listed pair that takes plural agreement. 'Either, or' would agree with the nearer subject (*assistants* — plural!) — but the pair 'Neither, or' is invalid English, and 'Not only, but' is incomplete without 'also'.
practice.shortcut: Verb agreement tiebreak: plural were with a full two-part subject → Both...and.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The minister gave a solemn ___ that the pending project would be cleared within a month.
practice.solution: A solemn statement meant to remove doubt is an **assurance** — the noun partner of *assure*. *Insurance* covers risk by policy, *endurance* is the power to bear hardship, *abundance* is plenty — none fits 'gave a solemn ___ that'.
